reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent, well-documented facts from multiple independent sites about Voyager 1's historic 1990 Family Portrait mosaic.
story: On Valentine's Day 1990, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft received a historic command: turn around and look back toward home. Cruising nearly four billion miles away and tilted 32 degrees above the planetary plane, Voyager pointed its optics inward. Astronomer Carl Sagan had campaigned for a decade for this final photo shoot before the probe's imaging system was powered down forever. Over 60 individual exposures, Voyager captured the first outside portrait of our planetary family. The mosaic framed six worlds—Jupiter, Earth, Venus, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—orbiting our Sun. Mercury and Mars were lost in the Sun's blinding glare, while Pluto was far too faint to detect. To prevent frying its delicate camera sensors, Voyager imaged the blazing central star through its darkest filter with an exposure of five thousandths of a second. From the outer solar frontier, Earth appeared as a fragile crescent smaller than a single pixel.
angle: Before shutting off its cameras forever, Voyager 1 turned around from nearly four billion miles away to photograph our entire Solar System, capturing Earth as a speck smaller than a single camera pixel.

claims.claim: Voyager 1 took the Family Portrait image sequence on February 14, 1990.
The image sequence was the first portrait ever taken of the Solar System from the outside.
Voyager 1 was selected over Voyager 2 because its trajectory had carried it above the plane of the Solar System.
Voyager 1 was positioned approximately 32 degrees above the ecliptic plane when it acquired the mosaic.
The spacecraft was approximately 3.7 to 4 billion miles (about 6 billion kilometers) away when taking the images.
The Family Portrait mosaic consists of a total of 60 individual photographic frames.
The mosaic incorporates 39 wide-angle camera frames linking the planets together.
Astronomer Carl Sagan campaigned for many years to get NASA to command the spacecraft to take these pictures.
The portrait frames were the final photographs ever captured by either Voyager spacecraft.
Six planets are visible across the mosaic: Jupiter, Earth, Venus, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
The Sun appears as a bright point of light within the mosaic.
Voyager photographed the Sun using its darkest filter to protect its vidicon tube sensors from saturation or damage.
The Sun was imaged using the shortest exposure time available to the camera.
Mercury was missed in the portrait because it was positioned too close to the Sun.
Mars was missed and could not be detected in the finished portrait.
Pluto was missed because its tiny size and vast distance left it too dim to be imaged.
Voyager 1 had a clear vantage point of Jupiter free from solar glare, whereas Jupiter was too close to the Sun from Voyager 2's vantage point.
Narrow-angle camera views were acquired to create close-up portraits of the individual planets.

disputed: Date of acquisition: Sources S1 and S2 list February 14, 1990, while S3 introduces 'February 15, 1990' near its conclusion after initially noting Valentine's Day. Script should state February 14, 1990.

Distance measurement: S1 and S3 state approximately 6 billion kilometers (3.7 billion miles), whereas S2 states approximately 4 billion miles. Script should state 'roughly four billion miles (six billion kilometers)'.

Reason Mars was missed: S1 attributes it to spacecraft viewing geometry creating a thin crescent and filter choice, whereas S3 simply groups Mars with Mercury as lost in solar glare. Script should state Mars was missed due to camera exposure limitations and solar glare.
